narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of accepted students, signaling that your later-year performance was weaker than most successful applicants. Your first-year class rank worked in the opposite direction and modestly improved the outlook, yet it was not strong enough to offset the third-year result.

Family income was the third most important factor and also nudged the prediction toward failure. You come from an upper-middle income background, which is the most common bracket among accepted students, but in this model it still contributed a small negative signal.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your solid undergraduate GPA of 3.40 (above the accepted average) and your LSAT score of 35 (only slightly below the accepted average of 37.18).

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program, and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
